sentences.text: The known skeleton belongs to a subadult individual estimated to be 1.5 meters long.
This lightly built, bipedal dinosaur possessed long legs for running and a rigid tail for balance.
It featured a short back with an avian sternum, an elongated neck, and a small, beaked skull adapted for eating plants.
The humerus is described as gracile and laterally bowed, though it remains fragmentary.
The ilium is slender, low, elongate, and displays a dorsally sigmoid outline shared with most basal ornithopods.
Fossils were collected in 2008 by Juan Moly and Rodolfo Coria from the Snow Hill Island Formation.
The species was formally described by Coria and colleagues in 2013 after remaining undescribed in the Museo de La Plata collections.
The genus name honors Argentine geologist Trinidad "Trini" Diaz and the Latin root for lizard.
The species name santamartaensis refers to Santa Marta Cove, the location where the fossils were found.
The holotype consists of a semi-articulated partial skeleton including vertebrae, an incomplete pelvis, a right humerus, and a partial right hindlimb.
Trinisaura exhibited a slower growth rate, likely an adaptation to the colder Antarctic climate.
The dinosaur evolved distinct traits due to geographic isolation after Antarctica broke off from Gondwana.
It was a herbivore with a long tail for balance, lithe hindlimbs, and short forelimbs.
A 2020 study analyzed the growth rates of Trinisaura and Morrosaurus using histological samples from their holotype long bones and third metatarsals.
Trinisaura is classified as a basal member of the ornithopod clade.
It is classified as an ornithopod dinosaur within the Neornithischia suborder.
Trinisaura belongs to the class Ornithischia.
The dinosaur belongs to the parent group Elasmaria.
Trinisaura lived in what is now James Ross Island off the coast of northern Antarctica.
It is part of a clade of ornithopod dinosaurs that links continents formerly part of Gondwana.
Trinisaura and Morrosaurus provide evidence of dinosaur ties between Antarctica and South America.
The animal lived approximately 72 million years ago during the late Campanian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Antarctica.
A 2022 analysis by Karen Poole found Trinisaura in the Rhabdodontoidea clade rather than in Elasmaria.
The discovery challenges the traditional view of southern continents as refugia by showing connected endemic ecosystems during the Cretaceous.
